title: push, pull and tracking branches
summary: Push publishes your commits only if it is a fast-forward for the server. Learn what rejection means and how pull --rebase keeps history clean.

steps.title: push and upstreams
body: git push -u origin feature/coupons   # first push: create it on origin, remember it as the upstream
git push                             # afterwards: push the current branch to its upstream

`-u` (`--set-upstream`) links your local branch to `origin/feature/coupons`. After that, plain `git push`, `git pull` and `git status` know which remote branch you mean. `git branch -vv` shows each branch's upstream.
The server accepts a push only if it is a **fast-forward** for its branch: its current tip must be an ancestor of what you send. Otherwise it would lose commits someone else pushed.

steps.prompt: You and a teammate both started from `origin/main` at B. They pushed C. You committed X locally and run `git push`. Git prints the line marked `???` for your branch. Write it, starting with `! [rejected]`, then the refs (`main -> main`) and the reason in parentheses.
code: error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:acme/shop.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
steps.explain: The server's main (C) is not an ancestor of your X, so accepting X would drop C. Git refuses. Fetch first, integrate, then push.

steps.title: pull: merge or rebase
body: After that rejection you need C in your branch. Two ways:
- `git pull` = fetch + **merge**: a merge commit M every time you were not up to date. Noisy history full of *Merge branch 'main' of github.com...*
- `git pull --rebase` = fetch + **rebase** your unpushed commits onto the new tip. Linear history, and safe because X was never pushed.
Most teams set `git config --global pull.rebase true`, or `pull.ff only` to make Git refuse anything but a fast-forward and decide each time.

steps.prompt: You were rejected because a teammate pushed first. Arrange the commands to integrate their work and publish yours with a linear history.
steps.explain: `git pull --rebase` does the first two in one go. Running the tests on the rebased result before pushing catches semantic conflicts with your teammate's change.

steps.prompt: During `git pull --rebase`, one of your commits conflicts. What do you do?
options: Resolve the file, `git add` it, `git rebase --continue`; or `git rebase --abort` to get back to before the pull
Commit the conflict markers and push
Run `git pull` again until it works
steps.explain: A pull --rebase is an ordinary rebase. Each of your commits is replayed, so you may resolve more than once.

steps.prompt: Match the command to its effect.
pairs: publish `topic` and remember `origin/topic` as its upstream
fetch, then replay my unpushed commits on top
show each branch's upstream and ahead/behind counts
delete the branch on the server

steps.prompt: Will the server accept a plain `git push`?
items: My branch has new commits; the server's tip is their ancestor
Someone else pushed since my last fetch
I amended a commit that was already pushed
I rebased my already-pushed branch onto main
I merged origin/main into my branch, then committed
steps.explain: Accepted means fast-forward: the server's tip is somewhere in your history. Amend and rebase replace pushed commits, so the old tip is no longer in your history.

steps.prompt: Complete the configuration so `git pull` always rebases, and new branches push to a same-named branch automatically.
steps.explain: `push.autoSetupRemote` makes the first plain `git push` of a new branch behave like `git push -u origin <branch>`.

steps.title: Will the push be accepted?
prompt: Model the server's check. Write `Push(string local, string remoteTip, parents, bool force)` returning:
starter: static string Push(string local, string remoteTip, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents, bool force)
solution: static HashSet<string> Ancestors(string start, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents)
static string Push(string local, string remoteTip, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents, bool force)
hints: The order of the checks matters: equality first.
template: Dojo.Eq("nothing to push", "Everything up-to-date", Push("C", "C", dojoG, false));
Dojo.Eq("new commits on top", "fast-forward", Push("E", "B", dojoG, false));
Dojo.Eq("someone else pushed first", "rejected (non-fast-forward)", Push("C", "E", dojoG, false));
Dojo.Eq("--force overwrites", "forced update", Push("C", "E", dojoG, true));
Dojo.Eq("pushing an older commit is rejected", "rejected (non-fast-forward)", Push("B", "E", dojoG, false));
